title: What time is it? What day is it?
title_target: Хэдэн цаг болж байна? Ямар гараг вэ?
goal: Tell the time, the day, and the date, and see why the Mongolian days of the week are seven heavenly bodies.
bekal: tell and ask the time, including half past and minutes past
name days, dates, and months, and make an appointment
use the time suffix *-д / -т* to say "at such-and-such o'clock"

dialogs.title: Яриа — Уулзалт товлох
dialogs.intro: Sarnai and Budi are arranging a time to go to the museum together. They're both busy, so it takes some back-and-forth.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Sarnai, what time shall we meet on Saturday?
lines.literal: Sarnai O, Saturday-on how-many hour-at meet Q?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Ten is too early. How about eleven?
lines.literal: ten early is. ten one hour-at may Q?

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Fine. What time does the museum open?
lines.literal: may. museum how-many hour-at open-usually Q?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: At the square. I'll get there at twenty past eleven.
lines.literal: square on. ten one hour twenty minute-at arrive.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Why twenty past? You said eleven!
lines.literal: why twenty minute-at Q? ten one-at so said you-know.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Sorry, the bus is slow. I'll try to make it by eleven.
lines.literal: sorry, bus slow go-usually. ten one-at arrive so try.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: No problem. I'm sometimes late too.
lines.literal: no-problem. I too also sometimes late-usually.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: What time are you going back? Do you have work in the evening?
lines.literal: how-many hour-at return Q? evening-at-own work-with Q?

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: I'll go home at half past three. I teach at four.
lines.literal: three hour half-at home-to-own return. four-at lesson teach.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Okay, got it. See you on Saturday, then!

notes: **Цаг means hour, time, and weather all at once.** *Хэдэн цаг вэ?* (what time is it), *цаг байхгүй* (there's no time), *цаг агаар* (weather). English "time" and "o'clock" grew from similar roots, so this overlap shouldn't feel strange.

⚠️ **The suffix -д / -т on a time means "at."** *Арван нэгэн цаг**т*** = at eleven o'clock. It's exactly the same suffix as the place suffix in unit 4: Mongolian treats time as a place, much like English says "**at** eleven" and "**at** home."

**Цагаас … хүртэл = from … until.** *Есөн цагаас зургаан цаг хүртэл*. The suffix *-аас* means "from" and works for both time and place, while *хүртэл* is a separate word that stands **after** the time.

**Гэж marks quotes and intentions.** *Арван нэгт **гэж** ярьсан* = "you said eleven"; *очих **гэж** хичээнэ* = "I'll try so as to arrive." This word is used constantly and has no single English equivalent: it's a spoken quotation mark.

**Хагас = half, and Mongolian counts forward, not back.** *Гурван цаг хагас* = "three hours and a half" = 3:30. ⚠️ This differs from German and Dutch, which say "half four" for 3:30, but **matches English** "half past three": you count forward from the hour that has passed.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: The pattern: **number with -н + цаг**, then the minutes if needed. To say "at such-and-such o'clock," add the suffix *-т* at the end.
after: ⚠️ *Дутуу* means "short of" and is used for minutes before the next hour, just like "to" in "quarter to four." In everyday speech people more often just say the minutes: *гурван цаг дөчин таван минут*.

**Mongolian doesn't use a twelve-hour system with "a.m./p.m." like English.** To be clear, add *өглөөний* (morning), *өдрийн* (daytime), *оройн* (evening), *шөнийн* (night, small hours) **before** the time: *оройн долоон цагт* = at seven in the evening.

grammars.title: Days, months, and dates
body: The Mongolian days of the week come from Tibetan and name seven heavenly bodies, the same pattern as the days in Japanese and Sanskrit (and in English Sunday, Monday, Saturday). Memorizing them as one series is much easier than as seven separate words.
after: ⚠️ The last column is the official form used in documents and schedules: "day one," "day two," and so on. In conversation people use the heavenly bodies. Both are common, so learn to recognize both.

**Months are named by number only: *нэгдүгээр сар* (first month = January), *хоёрдугаар сар* (February), up to *арван хоёрдугаар сар* (December).** That saves twelve words to memorize, and the system is the same as in Mandarin and Japanese. Dates: *арван тавны өдөр* or just *арван тавны*, "the fifteenth."

blocks.title: Making an appointment
items: *Хэзээ уулзах вэ?* — When shall we meet?
*Уучлаарай, тэр өдөр завгүй байна.* — Sorry, I'm busy that day.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: Last month I was in Ulaanbaatar.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice *ирэх* (coming) and *өнгөрсөн* (past) in the last two rows. Both are verb forms used as adjectives: *ирэх долоо хоног* literally means "the coming week," *өнгөрсөн сар* is "the month that passed." English does much the same with "the coming week" and "the past month," so the idea is already familiar.

A practical note on time in Mongolia: **office hours are usually 9:00–18:00 with a lunch break from 13:00 to 14:00, and that lunch break really is closed**: banks, post offices, and government offices lock their doors. If you have official business, ask *цайны цаг хэдэд вэ?* (when is the lunch break?) before you set out.

⚠️ Distinguish **цаг** (an hour) from **хоног** (a 24-hour day) and **өдөр** (a day as a day). *Гурван өдөр* and *гурван хоног* both mean "three days," but *хоног* stresses the length of time passing, while *өдөр* stresses the days themselves. For length of stay, visas, and trip length, Mongolians almost always use *хоног*.
